extracted.intended_audience: writers of flash/short creative nonfiction seeking markets for publication
extracted.subtask_description: A curated directory and guidance for where to submit very short creative nonfiction (flash). It lists journals, special sections, contests, and further reading relevant to placing flash nonfiction pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer journals that express specific interest in short prose
rubrics_metrics.description: This list points to journals that have expressed a specific interest in short prose; many literary journals will consider short prose whether they advertise that fact or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target publications that explicitly state they accept flash/nonfiction, but don't assume absence of an explicit statement means rejection — many journals will still consider short prose. Use this list as a starting point for venues that have signaled interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhere to journal length guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Several entries note preferred length or maximums for pieces (examples on the page: Guernica — 'fewer than 2,500'; NY Times Modern Love — 'a bit longer, 1500-1700 words'; presence of titles like '100 Word Story' and '82 Review' imply strict short-word limits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check individual journal submission pages for exact word counts and tailor your piece to those limits. Some venues specialize in very short pieces (100 words, flash), while others accept slightly longer personal essays; submitting outside stated ranges risks desk rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match thematic or topical focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Some outlets have explicit topical focuses (example: Obscura — 'nature focused'; Mslexia — 'UK based; “for women who write”').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing targets, align your subject matter and perspective with the journal's focus or audience. Read recent issues or guidelines to confirm fit; thematic mismatch reduces likelihood of acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conform to section- or column-specific tone and constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain publications accept pieces for named sections/columns with particular tone/angle (examples: The Christian Science Monitor’s 'Home Forum' section — '“upbeat” essays'; The Sun’s 'Readers Write' section; NY Times Modern Love has a characteristic length and tone).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If submitting to a regular column or reader-submission section, follow that column's tonal and structural conventions and any stated limits. Read sample entries from that section before submitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider contests and special calls for micro/flash work
rubrics_metrics.description: Some journals run contests or themed calls suited to flash work (example: Cincinnati Review (micro contest)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for contests or micro-specific calls that explicitly solicit flash nonfiction — these can be faster or more targeted paths to publication but may have entry fees or particular judging criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use recommended craft resources to refine flash nonfiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The page lists further resources and craft guides (examples: The Best of Brevity: Twenty Groundbreaking Years of Flash Nonfiction; The Rose Metal Press Field Guide to Writing Flash Nonfiction; Crafting the Personal Essay; interviews and Brevity Blog craft essays).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study specialized books, craft essays, and interviews about flash nonfiction to hone compression, voice, and structural choices unique to the form before submitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read editors' and craft essays to learn submission expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Brevity links to craft discussions and essays on the writing life and includes blog posts that deepen craft and editorial perspective (e.g., 'Flash Nonfiction: An Interview with Dinty W. Moore'; Brevity Blog entries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage with editorial commentary and craft posts to understand what editors value in flash nonfiction — what counts as effective compression, memorable openings, and satisfying endings at very short lengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broaden search using curated magazine/journal databases
rubrics_metrics.description: The page points readers to broader tools for finding markets (example: Literary Magazines and Journals Database from Poets & Writers; filter by 'creative nonfiction').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use database filters (genre, length, region) to discover additional venues beyond curated lists and to verify up-to-date submission guidelines and editorial focus.
